data.title: US urges China to meet rare earths, agriculture commitments ahead of Trump-Xi meetings
data.description:
[WASHINGTON] The Trump administration warned a top Chinese official on Friday (Nov 6) that Beijing must immediately implement its commitments under a nearly year-old trade agreement, particularly on delivery of rare earths and other critical minerals and agricultural purchases, the US Trade Representative’s Office (USTR) said.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer urged Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng in a call to implement terms of the pact agreed in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025, the US agencies said.

“During the call, Ambassador Greer emphasised the critical importance of China taking concrete actions to fully implement its past commitments, particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals,” USTR said in a statement.

During the call, China expressed “serious concern” over recent US trade restrictions targeting Beijing, China’s official Xinhua news agency said.

But He, China’s lead negotiator on trade relations with the US, agreed with his US counterparts to continue using consultation for “stable and positive” development of trade ties, Xinhua reported.

US Presidents Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are expected to meet at the summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, China, on Nov 18 and 19, and the G-20 summit in Miami on Dec 14 and 15.

Greer said the Trump administration will pursue balanced trade with China by “monitoring compliance of past commitments while unlocking lasting benefits for American farmers, ranchers, manufacturers, and workers”.

Greer, Bessent and other US officials have frequently complained about difficulties that US companies say they are experiencing in receiving sufficient quantities of rare earths and other critical minerals from China under the Busan agreement.

The US says the deal was designed to lift restrictions put in place in 2025 during a period of tariff escalations between the world’s two largest economies.

The Busan trade deal, which expires on Jan 10, capped US tariffs on Chinese goods implemented during Trump’s second term at about 20 per cent. China has pledged to buy 25 million tonnes of US soybeans for the next three years and boost purchases of other American farm goods by US$17 billion.

“I emphasised the importance of China fully and immediately honouring its commitments, raised concerns about recent Chinese actions and underscored that progress depends on concrete results,” Bessent said in a social media post.

The US will “closely assess China’s implementation of the arrangement,” the Treasury said in a statement.

Beijing has signalled tariff concessions remain central to its aims, with its commerce ministry saying on Thursday that China was open to buying more US farm goods, but only if the two sides implement their reciprocal tariff-cut agreement.

Following a September summit between Xi and Trump in Washington, the two sides proposed a US$60 billion package of reciprocal tariff cuts, including roughly US$17 billion worth of US farm goods that China imported in 2024, though the plan has not been finalised.

The White House said in May that Beijing had agreed to buy US$17 billion of US agricultural goods annually from 2026, with this year’s target adjusted on a prorated basis. Those purchases were in addition to a commitment made in October last year to buy US soybeans. REUTERS

data.title: US: Wall Street stocks rally after heavy AI-relatedÂ sell-off
data.description:
[NEW YORK] Wall Street equities mostly rallied on Friday (Nov 6), reversing course after trillions of dollars of world stock market value were wiped out over fears that Democratic election victories this week would bring tighter US regulations for the artificial intelligence industry.

The benchmark S&P 500 and the Nasdaq finished higher, with technology, communication services and industrials stocks driving gains. The Dow ended lower. All three indices notched weekly losses following a brutal sell-off in the prior session.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.5 per cent, the S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.1 per cent.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index was up 4.2 per cent after slumping in its biggest one-day drop since April 2025. Nvidia rose nearly 3 per cent, after its worst day since January 2025, when the emergence of low-cost Chinese AI model DeepSeek hammered markets.

Other heavyweight chipmakers, including AMD, Intel and Micron Technology, closed up between 5 and 11 per cent, while Elon Musk’s Tesla and SpaceX were also up 4 per cent and nearly 9 per cent, respectively, after losses earlier this week.

“Most of the disruption of the AI build-out will not probably occur but it’s just the uncertainty of the change in government from Republican-led to Democratic-led, not only at the federal level but the state, local levels,” said Gerry Sparrow, president and portfolio manager at Sparrow Capital Management.

“That’s causing some disruption in the expectations of investors... The volatility around elections or any political event, whether it be war or terrorist attack, is always going to disrupt the market.”

Texas’ Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa said on Thursday that the state – which already has a large share of US data centres – will introduce new laws to protect local communities from their further mass buildup.

The jitters are hitting an AI trade already under pressure from fears that the massive cost of the data centres and other infrastructure will limit future returns, spurring margin calls and spooking retail investors and hedge funds alike.

The bounces were in stark contrast with market action in the rest of the world. Europe’s Stoxx 600 lost 1 per cent.

In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi both slumped about 6 per cent. For the Nikkei – just like Wall Street the previous day – it was the biggest one-day drop since US President Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” trade tariff panic of April 2025.

The MSCI All-World index fell 0.7 per cent while MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan lost nearly 3 per cent.

US non-farm payrolls, usually one of the most-watched pieces of data, but largely overshadowed by the tech drama, showed a stronger-than-expected 165,000 pickup in jobs.

The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note ticked up to 4.86 per cent, having dropped to its lowest level since Sep 9 overnight.

Brent crude prices settled at US$98.32, rising just 0.03 per cent, on hopes the midterms’ results might prompt Trump to de-escalate the Iran war.

Spot gold was flat at US$4,066.28 per ounce. REUTERS

data.title: Retirement, a ârule of thirdsâ and what you cannot plan for
data.description:
RETIREMENT can be a vulnerable chapter for some, an exciting one for others, and a beautiful new beginning for those who are ready.

Some people barely think about it until it arrives. I started reflecting on it in my 40s, and two experiences shaped my thinking.

My father retired in his early 60s after a demanding and often stressful working life. Without a clear purpose beyond work, he largely went with the flow. His social circle was small, limited mostly to extended family.

By his mid 70s, dementia had begun to take hold, progressively worsening until he died during the Covid-19 years.

Watching his decline taught me something about the importance of intentionality, staying engaged and having something meaningful to live for beyond work.

In my early 40s, I was the chief operating officer of a company in the Philippines, reporting to a CEO I deeply admired. He believed that businesses had a responsibility to contribute to society. He often spoke about his plans to give back to the community and mentor others when he eventually retired.

Many colleagues and friends have shared similar aspirations, always prefaced by “when I retire”. These would include travelling more, getting healthier, volunteering, doing charity work and spending more time with family.

Their putting these things off into the distant future troubled me.

Why must we wait until retirement to do the things that give our lives meaning? Why not weave them into our lives while we are still working?

Purpose shaped by experience

An unlikely beginning in life has shaped my purpose.

I was a junior-college dropout in Singapore. Through the encouragement and support of teachers and friends who believed in me, I eventually made it to university and built a successful career.

That experience left me with an enduring desire to help others realise their potential.

Later, working in the Philippines and Australia exposed me to poverty, inequality and social injustices unlike what anyone would experience in Singapore. It broadened my purpose to include helping businesses contribute to societal progress.

By my mid-40s, two convictions guided me: enabling people’s potential and creating positive social impact.

The question was how to sustain that purpose through my full-time corporate career and beyond it.

My “rule of thirds”

Earlier in my career, leading corporate strategy and venture capital, I learnt to think across three horizons: strengthen today’s business, build tomorrow’s growth, and invest in possibilities beyond that.

No business should place all its bets on one future. Diversification, optionality and adaptability create resilience when circumstances change.

Over time, I adopted my own rule of thirds, applying it to finances, leadership, career development and, eventually, retirement.

It was never mathematical precision I sought, but a practical approach to balancing competing priorities and trade-offs without making things too complicated and becoming overwhelmed.

Financial freedom through diversification

I aimed to save at least a third of my after-tax income, investing those savings over time across three asset classes: fixed deposits, equities and property.

Even within these, I diversified. Fixed deposits had different maturities and currencies; equities and superannuation spanned different risk and tenure profiles; property investments covered different markets.

There was no magic in these allocations. They were not meant for complete optimisation, nor did I try to time markets.

They provided something more valuable to me: peace of mind, passive income over time, and the freedom to make career choices without being driven by money.

Moving into corporate sustainability, which was nascent in 2013, required me to take a significant cut in my overall remuneration. But financial security allowed me to prioritise purpose.

Building career optionality before needing it

My career also evolved through three broad chapters: early career and middle management, senior leadership across businesses and geographies and, finally, purpose-led work in sustainability and leadership development.

Within my last corporate role, I deliberately developed three career horizons.

The first was my core responsibility and full-time role, leading corporate sustainability.

The second was leadership coaching, which I began developing professionally in 2013 on the side. Over time, I coached more leaders and mentored CEOs and social entrepreneurs through corporate community programmes.

In the final third, I began preparing for board and governance roles, investing in the knowledge, contribution, credentials and networks needed.

I could not do everything at once. New competence takes time to build; credibility, trust and reputation take even longer.

But by progressively investing a fraction of my time in future possibilities, I was not starting from scratch when the time came to eventually leave corporate life.

I was building my next chapter while still living the present one.

Repurposing, not retiring

After 36 years with Singtel, I stepped away from full-time corporate employment in March 2026.

Rather than retiring in the conventional sense, I saw the change as taking my purpose to new intersections – or repurposing.

In this new chapter, a third of my time is for family, health, travel and simply enjoying greater freedom; a third for coaching; and a third for board and governance work aligned with my purpose.

Coaching also went three ways: commercial coaching for senior executives; discounted coaching for women and leaders from under-represented backgrounds; and pro-bono coaching for displaced mature workers who struggled to return to employment.

My board commitments similarly focus on social impact, including at Singapore’s National Council of Social Service, a social enterprise supporting vulnerable youth and employability across Asia, and an upcoming one in Australia's not-for-profit sector.

The same purpose, expressed through different contributions.

When life changes the plan

Just as I was finding momentum in this new chapter, life took an unexpected turn. I was diagnosed with prostate cancer.

Surgery followed, and recovery has required me to reconsider my priorities and pace.

It was a sobering reminder that however carefully we plan, life owes us no certainty.

Yet, this is also where thinking in thirds has served me. A diversified portfolio of commitments gives me the flexibility to rebalance, slow down or redirect my energies without losing my sense of purpose.

The proportions may change but the purpose need not.

This rule of thirds is not science; it will not suit everyone. What it has given me is a way to manage uncertainty without trying to control everything.

Perhaps the greatest lesson from watching my father, and now facing my own mortality, is that we should not postpone living purposefully until we have finished working.

Retirement need not be the moment we discover what matters. It can simply be another intersection at which we choose how to express what should have mattered all along.

We can start doing now what we envisage for the future, whether we are retired or not.

The writer is the CEO and founder of Human Meridian Advisory, a board, leadership and career advisory firm.

The financial arrangements described reflect the writer’s personal experience and circumstances and should not be construed as professional advice.

Switching Lanes is a column exploring the diverse realities of life after a full-time career. From finding fresh purpose to savouring newfound freedom, we are redefining retirement.

Have a perspective to share? Write to btletter@sph.com.sg with the subject, Switching Lanes.

data.title: Stocks to watch: DBS, CAReit, Starhill Global Reit, Koh Brothers Eco Engineering
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 5):

DBS : The lender reported on Thursday a net profit of S$2.81 billion for the three months ended Sep 30, down 5 per cent from S$2.95 billion in the year-ago period. DBS said earnings growth was offset by lower markets trading income amid unfavourable equity market conditions. The latest net profit fell short of the S$2.95 billion consensus forecast from a Bloomberg survey of eight analysts. DBS also announced that its chairman, Peter Seah, will retire at the end of this year, with board member Anthony Lim set to succeed him from Jan 1, 2027. Shares of DBS ended 0.1 per cent or S$0.10 lower at S$70.78 on Wednesday.

Centurion Accommodation Reit (CAReit) : The real estate investment trust (Reit) on Wednesday posted net property income of S$117.7 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, coming in 4.8 per cent above its prospectus forecast. Its manager said the better-than-expected performance was helped by higher rental rates at its Singapore worker dormitories and new bed capacity. Revenue came in at S$164.4 million, 5.7 per cent ahead of the S$155.6 million forecast in the Reit’s initial public offering prospectus dated Sep 18, 2025. Units of CAReit ended 1.9 per cent or S$0.02 higher at S$1.07 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Starhill Global Reit : The Reit manager said that Australian retailer David Jones, which is the anchor tenant at its Perth property David Jones Building, verbally informed the trust that it has entered into voluntary administration. The lease contributed to around 4.7 per cent of the Reit’s total portfolio revenue for the financial year ended Jun 30. Assuming the tenant’s lease ended on Jul 1, 2025, with no replacement for 12 months, the Reit’s distribution per unit for FY2025 would be around S$0.0329, compared to the actual S$0.0368, on a pro forma basis. The counter closed 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.51.

Koh Brothers Eco Engineering: The engineering solutions group said on Wednesday that it plans to raise up to S$27.6 million through a renounceable underwritten rights issue, with its parent committing to subscribe for its full entitlement. Koh Brothers Eco Engineering, which recently transferred from Catalist to Singapore Exchange’s mainboard, will offer up to 563,644,184 new shares at S$0.049 each, on the basis of one rights share for every five existing shares held. The counter ended 15.9 per cent or S$0.011 lower at S$0.058 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

data.title: National powerlifter, meal preparation firmâs founder bag Berita Harian awards
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Despite breaking multiple world records, national powerlifter Farhanna Farid is proudest when she helps others beat their personal bests.

“When my athletes or clients break their own personal records, I think that achievement actually far supersedes my own world records because I feel like I have managed to make a difference to someone,” said Farhanna, 34, who is also a personal coach.

The former pharmacist is also working to help relieve the financial strain of athletes in her role as an executive committee member of Powerlifting Singapore, where she leads marketing and sponsorship.

For her sporting achievements – she has earned 14 world records – and dedication to elevating women in sports, Farhanna received the Berita Harian Achiever of the Year 2026 award on Friday (Nov 6).

Now in their 28th year, the awards, organised by the Malay-language daily and sponsored by Maybank, recognise Malay/Muslim individuals who have made a mark in their fields.

In the past year, Farhanna has achieved sporting success. She placed fifth overall in the World Classic Open Powerlifting Championships in June, competing against top athletes from New Zealand, the Netherlands, Canada and the US.

Her achievements have inspired other women to take up the sport – Farhanna said one of her teammates took up powerlifting after reading her interview with women’s magazine Cleo.

In September, Farhanna also organised Lift Like A Girl, a women-only competition.

She said: “I hope this award serves as a reminder that we should never be afraid to challenge ourselves, embrace who we are and pursue what truly matters to us.

“Because sometimes, when we find the courage to believe in ourselves, we give others the courage to do the same.”

Education Minister Desmond Lee, who was the guest of honour at the award ceremony at Four Seasons Hotel Singapore, said the winners are role models for all Singaporeans.

“When those of us fortunate enough to have done well choose to support others and pay it forward, we create a virtuous cycle that strengthens our communities and our nation,” he said.

Lee also gave out the Berita Harian Young Achiever of the Year 2026 award to entrepreneur Nabill Shukry Johary, in recognition of his resilience in overcoming financial hardship to build a thriving business.

In July 2021, with just S$1,000 in personal savings, Nabill and his father launched Cheekies, which sells marinated, preservative-free meat.

His family, living in a one-room public rental flat in Tampines, has faced financial hardship over the years.

His parents, who ran an interior design company from 2000 to 2004, had to shut down the firm after their business partner ran off with company funds. His mother also had to stop work in 2003 due to psoriatic arthritis.

His father, who became a private-hire driver, struggled during the Covid-19 pandemic when customers were few.

Drawing on lessons learnt from difficult times, Nabill persevered through any difficulties that Cheekies faced, including in 2022 when Malaysia banned the export of chicken to Singapore.

Cheekies now produces up to 500 kg of pre-marinated meats weekly and is expanding into Malaysia in 2027.

Nabill also in September pledged S$10,000 to start a bursary at his alma mater, Republic Polytechnic, for struggling students.

The driving force behind his ambition was to purchase a home for his mother. She died in March.

“My mum always wanted to see me win an award. In my five years of business, we have never won an award before. I think she would be very proud,” said Nabill, who will receive a trophy and S$3,000.

Berita Harian and Maybank also introduced a new award category: the BH-Maybank Perkasa award, which recognises two Singaporeans of any race who have overcome socio-economic challenges to achieve success.

The inaugural awardees, who will each receive a trophy and S$3,000, were Siti Nurhumaira Azman and Elizabeth Neo.

Berita Harian editor Nazry Mokhtar said: “We are opening this award to all races because next year is our 70th anniversary. This is a huge milestone for us, and we felt it is a good time for us to open new doors. It shows that our community is ready to stand with everyone to celebrate everyday resilience.”

Neo, 37, a social work associate at the Fellowship of Men Singapore, helps to build safer families and strengthen their emotional resilience.

She said she draws on her decade-long struggle with addiction and incarceration to provide emotional support and empathy.

Humaira, 26, who grew up in a one-room rental flat in Ang Mo Kio with seven siblings, her mother and her grandparents, said she reached her lowest point in April when her eight-month-old son died.

He was diagnosed with spinal muscular atrophy at four months, a diagnosis which came with a hefty S$2.4 million treatment option.

The public policy officer at the Ministry of Law said: “I see this award as a symbol of hope... This award is something to push people and let them know they can also achieve if they push through.” THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: Issue 219: Singapore sharpens haze law; South-east Asiaâs blended sweet spots
data.description:
Environmental policy

Haze law’s new teeth must bite

On paper, changes to Singapore’s transboundary haze law sharpen the teeth of the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act (THPA). But the threat of getting bitten will not improve behaviour in the palm oil industry until authorities demonstrate that they can hold companies and individuals accountable for causing this year’s haze.

Singapore Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu told Parliament on Wednesday (Nov 4) that the THPA amendments are aimed at giving the country “better ways to obtain and verify information, trace complex corporate relationships, and impose meaningful consequences on errant entities, even where criminal prosecution proves difficult”.

The changes are a welcome move in the right direction to sharpen the THPA.

For instance, one change will empower the director-general of environmental protection to direct entities suspected of links to haze pollution to appoint approved expert private-sector assessors at their own expense. These assessors will establish relevant facts, leaving it to the authorities to decide on enforcement and the courts to determine liability.

This means palm oil players could now be subject to what is effectively a mandatory audit as long as they are under suspicion for liability in haze pollution. While the current regime’s teeth will bite only when authorities can establish liability – which has proven to be extremely challenging given the complexities of investigating and prosecuting a foreign entity – the new rules significantly lower the barrier for palm oil players to face enforcement action. Furthermore, the imposition of external investigators makes it easier for liability – if it exists – to be discovered.

The new rules also allow the government to target supply chains connected to liable entities. The Singapore government will be able to restrict business dealings with designated entities and individuals that have been convicted under the haze law on penalty of fines. Entities with relevant connections to activities associated with burning, such as large forestry and agriculture companies, may also be ordered to ensure that their supply chains do not involve entities that cause such fires.

A palm oil player is therefore potentially on the hook for its whole supply chain. That risk will also get transferred to its suppliers, financiers and insurers, and therefore raise the cost of doing business for the palm oil company.

One other important change tightens the definition of responsible behaviour within the Act. The original Act gave an accused three defences: If a fire was due to natural disaster or an act of war, if the fire was caused by another party without the accused entity’s knowledge, or if the accused took reasonable steps to prevent and put out the fire. The amendments combine the latter two, such that an accused will have to prove not just that the fire was caused by another party without its knowledge, but that the accused also took reasonable preventive and firefighting measures. A new civil penalty framework will make it easier for the authorities to mete out punishment when liability is determined.

In sum, the amendments to the haze law will probably make it substantially easier for authorities to obtain information about a palm oil player’s connections to haze-causing fires, and then to go after an entity when liability is determined.

That threat is important. If suspicion is enough to expose the company to an external assessment, and if liability leads to actual economic costs, palm oil companies will make the calculus that it is better to play by the rules, and to be transparent enough that suppliers, customers, financiers, insurers and investors are sufficiently assured to do business without demanding a risk premium.

The share prices of Singapore-listed palm oil companies have mostly fallen sharply since the haze began and Singapore began to toughen its stance. But markets have short memories, and when this haze season eventually blows over and demand for palm oil continues to grow, and the industry’s own sustainability body comes up with stronger standards that everyone claims to be following, palm oil prices will recover and so will share prices, and burning practices will continue until the next major haze episode triggers a new round of indignance.

To bring about actual change, the regulatory threat must be real and durable. Getting there will require this round of assessments to lead to meaningful sanctions against those responsible for the haze. Otherwise we will be back where we started, with a set of laws that do not work.

It remains to be seen whether the THPA amendments will be enough. Much hinges on the extent to which the assessors can connect the fires responsible for the haze to the people and entities ultimately responsible for those fires. It will not be an easy task. If liability exists, those liable are highly incentivised to ensure that they can claim they are not related to those who caused the fires, that the fires occurred without their knowledge, and that they took reasonable preventive and fire control measures. It is a cat and mouse game, and the mouse is typically a very good player.

But until the cat can catch a mouse, the mice will have little reason to fear its teeth.

Sustainable finance

Batteries, solar offer blended pathways in South-east Asia

Blended finance can seem like a miraculous financial solution that turns on the faucets of capital for unbankable projects.

However, what makes blended finance “blended” – the use of concessional capital to mobilise private capital within a single investment – also imposes constraints that limit use cases for the solution. Deals must deliver impact and financial “additionality” – financing can be obtained only with the help of non-commercial capital – to satisfy concessional funders, as well as profits to satisfy private investors.

A new report by blended finance group Convergence and the International Energy Agency explores how to best apply blended finance in South-east Asia, particularly Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam.

In Indonesia, rooftop solar and decentralised energy solutions could be the sweet spot where scale and risk mitigation are most needed. Credit guarantees by concessional financiers can reduce lender exposure to borrower or project-level risks, thereby enabling longer tenors or lower collateral requirements for aggregating larger projects.

In Vietnam, battery storage and offshore wind are nascent sectors where blended finance can catalyse early deployment and establish scalable financing structures.

The report notes that blended finance cannot remove all financing hurdles, and that policy, regulatory and system-level reforms must also take place.

“Bankability rests on clear contractual arrangements, predictable remuneration frameworks, and transparent procurement procedures, which remain incomplete” in the markets examined in the report. Physical readiness, including transmission and distribution networks and port infrastructure for battery storage and offshore wind, are key for unlocking investments in those sectors as well. Furthermore, counterparty exposure limits and limited long-term currency hedging hinder finance availability.

“Blended finance can cushion the effects of these constraints where they translate into identifiable project-level risks, but it cannot resolve them,” the report states. “Sustained mobilisation of private capital depends on durable policy reforms, credible market frameworks, improved power system readiness, and deeper domestic financing capacities.”

  • Singapore to ratify Asean haze coordination centre agreement ‘in the next few days’: Grace Fu
  • ‘Energy nationalism’ in Asean: Businesses face risks, but can’t ignore the opportunities
  • Markets are pushing electrification. Governments must push harder
  • Stronger governance code, listing rules need backing of a robust culture of stewardship

data.title: Everything, bar the kitchen sink, to upend trans-Pacific sea trade
data.description:
EVEN as the tariffs war between China and US escalates, another perhaps more damaging clash looms on the horizon. The United States Trade Representative (USTR), the agency that sets Washington’s trade policies, has proposed a series of restrictions and levies that could upend trans-Pacific trade. The Trump administration will make a final decision next month.

Inter alia, USTR proposes levies of up to US$1.5 million on any Chinese-built vessels entering American ports. About 17 per cent of all container vessels calling at US ports are Chinese-made. Further, such a levy would effectively stop all of China’s state-owned Cosco container ships from calling at US ports. There will be additional fees on any shipping firm that has orders for Chinese-made vessels. Based on the percentage of vessels ordered from Chinese shipyards, additional fees would range from US$500,000 to US$1million per vessel entrance.

In the quaint language of the USTR, it wants to “obtain (sic) the elimination of China’s acts, policies, and practices ... in light of China’s market power over global supply, pricing and access in the maritime, logistics and shipbuilding sectors…”. To fix this perceived problem, the USTR proposes throwing everything, bar the proverbial kitchen sink, to wreck China’s dominant position in shipbuilding; in transporting goods by sea; as well as in making containers and the kit that moves containers from rail or road onto ships and back again.

The agency notes that China’s shipbuilding market share grew from less than 5 per cent in 1999 to more than 50 per cent in 2023. Additionally, the Asian country’s ownership of the global commercial fleet grew to more than 19 per cent by January 2024. And Beijing accounts for 95 per cent of container production.

The USTR wants the percentage of US goods required to be transported on US-flagged vessels to increase gradually, starting at 1 per cent and reaching 15 per cent over seven years. One estimate for orders for new merchant vessels puts China well ahead of the pack with 61 per cent, Japan and South Korea with 12 per cent each, and Europe with 5 per cent.

The agency cites chapter and verse on why this dominance by China could displace foreign firms, reduce competition and create dependencies. While concern for Washington’s position in sea-borne commerce is the USTR’s ostensible reason, there is almost certainly a military dimension to this. America’s current shipbuilding capacity is almost entirely devoted to its navy. It is plagued by a limited number of shipyards, shortage of skilled workers, and consequently, cost blowouts and delays in delivery. Last year, the US Navy forecasted long delays for its warship modernisation programme. Washington is well aware how the atrophy of its commercial shipbuilding capacity has spilled over to its warship building programme. At the same time, Chinese warships are becoming a match for the US fleet.

That said, it should be noted that China’s shipbuilding capacity rests on weak foundations. Most engines for its merchant vessels come from Japan, Germany or Finland. It has been reported that there are perhaps only four firms in the world that can make crankshafts for these giant merchant vessels – namely Italy’s HSD Mechatronics, Hyundai Heavy Industries of Korea, Sidenor of Spain and Kobe Steel of Japan.

Expect Washington to arm-twist its allies, such as they are, to cut off supply of vital components bound for China. Counter-strikes will follow. If you thought Houthis in the Red Sea were bad for trade, you ain’t seen nothing yet.

data.title: US recession odds are becoming unsettlingly high
data.description:
THE notion of a US recession seemed remote just a few months ago, a mere blip on the radar of economic possibilities. More recently, however, that picture has started to change. A downturn, while still a risk scenario, is no longer unthinkable. A confluence of factors, from policy uncertainties to fragile financial markets, is casting a shadow over the world’s largest economy.

Several key financial indicators are already flashing yellow. The yield on 10-year Treasury bonds has fallen about 70 basis points in recent weeks, while oil prices have slipped below US$70 a barrel. These moves coincide with a string of disappointing economic data releases, reflecting growing apprehension about the immediate consequences of President Donald Trump’s trade policies and public sector reforms. Indeed, judging from recent surveys, policy uncertainties have already dampened business and household confidence, clouding the economic outlook. This spreading weakness is manifesting itself in three distinct stages.

First, lower-income households have been struggling, burdened by dwindling savings, maxed-out credit cards and mounting debt. Second, the corporate sector is now adopting more of a wait-and-see approach, faced with a barrage of policy pronouncements and an increasingly unpredictable environment. Third, the threat of a tit-for-tat tariff war has become much more of a reality this week, with the potential to disrupt global supply chains and stifle economic growth.

Adding to the unease, inflation, which had shown signs of abating, is proving more stubborn than anticipated. This whiff of stagflation – that troublesome combination of stagnant growth and rapidly rising prices – raises the spectre of another policy misstep by the Federal Reserve. The central bank faces a delicate balancing act as it’s caught between the requirements of its dual mandate to maximise employment and deliver price stability.

Not a foregone conclusion

Yet, it is important to remember that recession is, at this stage, far from a foregone conclusion. Several factors offer a counterweight to these negative forces.

Lower energy prices boost the purchasing power of consumers and reduce input costs for businesses. The administration’s deregulation agenda could unleash a wave of corporate investment. And, while the short-term disruptions caused by Trump’s trade policies are undeniable, the potential for long-term productivity gains through innovation in areas such as artificial intelligence, robotics and life sciences should not be discounted. Similarly, if handled well, public sector reforms could open the way for more efficient government operations and even provide some debt relief.

Nevertheless, the balance of risks has shifted. It is just a matter of time until economic forecasters revise down their 2025 growth projections from the median estimate of 2.3 per cent in a February Bloomberg survey. A downward revision of as much as a full percentage point is not out of the question, raising concern about how far the US economy is from “stall speed”.

While still relatively low, my probability of a recession has increased from 10 per cent at the beginning of the year to 25 to 30 per cent today. This is a consequential and quite unsettling development for an economy with high potential and aspirations, elevated asset prices, and a pivotal role in driving global growth.

A former chief executive officer of Pimco, the writer is president of Queens’ College, Cambridge; chief economic adviser at Allianz; and chair of Gramercy Funds Management. He is author of The Only Game in Town.

data.title: Malaysia attorney general intervenes to halt ex-PM Najibâs house arrest transfer
data.description:
[KUALA LUMPUR] Malaysia’s attorney general on Friday (Nov 6) postponed jailed former premier Najib Razak’s transfer to house arrest to review his royal pardon, in a last-minute intervention after a court cleared him to leave prison four years into his sentence.

Najib, prime minister from 2009 to 2018, was jailed in relation to a multibillion-dollar scandal at state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) and was granted approval in a September royal pardon to serve his remaining two years at home.

A court gave Najib the green light earlier on Friday to start his house arrest and he left prison briefly to undergo a scheduled dental checkup, Transport Minister Anthony Loke said.

Police and throngs of media had gathered for most of the day outside Najib’s cordoned-off Kuala Lumpur residence in anticipation of his arrival.

But the Attorney-General’s Chambers late on Friday said questions had arisen over the legal interpretation of King Sultan Ibrahim’s pardon and the court order allowing Najib to leave jail.

“In this regard, the implementation of house arrest... should be temporarily suspended until further investigation and clarification,” it said in a three-page statement.

‘Executive overreach’

Najib’s legal team said there was no lawful reason to keep him in jail in disregard of a royal order, adding the attorney general had been present at a meeting that advised the king on the pardon and had raised no concerns.

“To claim the power to suspend His Majesty’s order by media statement is, in our view, executive overreach,” it said.

One of Malaysia’s most influential and divisive politicians, Najib has repeatedly denied wrongdoing in the 1MDB case and insists he was made the scapegoat for the ⁠complex, globe-spanning scheme that siphoned away as much as US$4.5 billion, according to US investigators.

More than US$1 billion allegedly ended up in accounts linked to Najib, 1MDB’s co-founder, prosecutors have said.

He was also convicted of abuse of power and money laundering in a separate 1MDB-related case in December and sentenced to 15 years in prison with fines of US$2.8 billion. He has appealed that verdict.

Najib was given a boost earlier on Friday when his party, the United Malays National Organisation (Umno), paid a RM50 million (US$12.3 million) fine on his behalf, raised through crowdfunding, to allow him to leave prison, which was a condition of his pardon.

In a statement under a headline that said “do not commit treason”, Umno’s secretary-general Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki said the pardon must be respected.

“What justification is there for further delaying the implementation of house arrest?” he said.

Najib was for years a towering figure in Malaysian politics and still commands influence in Umno, which is part of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s multi-party government.

Anwar’s Pakatan Harapan alliance has strongly opposed leniency towards Najib, putting it at odds with the once dominant Umno, and his transfer to house arrest could create more political tension.

It is also likely to fuel criticism over the government’s handling of corruption cases and further erode support for Anwar after setbacks in two state elections this year, which went the way of Umno.

Though the next general election is not due until early 2028, Anwar has said he could call a snap poll if rifts deepen.

Loke, leader of the Democratic Action Party (DAP), the largest member of Anwar’s ruling bloc, on Friday said he would resign from the Cabinet as soon as Najib begins house arrest.

Former DAP lawmaker Tony Pua, who played a key role in uncovering the 1MDB scandal, said Najib was “Malaysia’s biggest crook” and chided Umno for fundraising to get him out of prison.

“Instead of using such a large sum of money to help ordinary Malaysians, they chose to ‘free’ Malaysia’s most corrupt,” he said on Facebook. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: OCBC, IHH Healthcare, FLCT, SingPost, Koh Brothers Eco Engineering
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 6):

OCBC : The lender reported on Friday a 3 per cent rise in net profit for its third quarter amid strong performance across its wealth management and wholesale banking businesses. This was despite lower profit contributions from its insurance arm Great Eastern. Net profit for the three months ended Sep 30 stood at S$2.04 billion, compared with S$1.98 billion in the year-ago period. Shares of OCBC ended 0.3 per cent or S$0.08 higher at S$27.93 on Thursday.

IHH Healthcare : The healthcare group, which has a secondary listing on the Singapore Exchange, announced on Thursday that close to 400 employees will be leaving the organisation as part of efforts to consolidate its business support services. The affected employees are based in Singapore, Hong Kong and Malaysia. Some employees will be moved into redesigned roles, while around 0.5 per cent of IHH’s total workforce of 76,000 will transition out of the organisation across the three markets. IHH shares ended flat at S$2.45 on Thursday, ahead of the announcement.

Frasers Logistics & Commercial Trust (FLCT) : The real estate investment trust’s distribution per unit (DPU) remained unchanged at S$0.0295 for the second half ended September, as an increase in DPU before capital distributions from divestment gains was offset by lower distributions from such gains. The manager expects borrowing costs to rise in FY2027, reflecting higher interest rates on variable-rate borrowings and debt due for refinancing. Units of FLCT ended Thursday 1.7 per cent or S$0.015 higher at S$0.925.

SingPost : The company on Friday posted a 183.7 per cent rise in net profit to S$55.9 million for the first half ended Sep 30, from S$19.7 million a year earlier, largely driven by exceptional gains from property divestments. Revenue slipped 1.3 per cent to S$185.9 million from S$188.4 million, mainly due to lower international revenue amid a structural decline in letter mail volumes. Underlying net profit more than doubled to S$11.5 million from S$5.5 million, supported by improved operating performance and a tax provision write-back. Shares of SingPost closed 1.8 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.29 on Thursday.

Koh Brothers Eco Engineering: The engineering solutions group said on Thursday that a former subcontractor, who commenced a claim in August against Koh Brothers Building & Civil Engineering Contractor (KBCE), a wholly owned subsidiary, and chairman Koh Keng Siang, discontinued its claims against the latter, with no order as to costs. However, the former subcontractor’s claims against KBCE and KBCE’s counterclaim against the claimant remain ongoing. The group said it will update its shareholders on any material developments. Its counter ended 5.2 per cent or S$0.003 lower at S$0.055 on Thursday, before the announcement.
